1:
The opening clause is disputed before anything else is. Clarke holds that it certainly belongs to the preceding chapter, and is so placed by the Vulgate, the Septuagint, the Syriac and the Arabic. Henry reads it the same way: the first words seem to have no reference to the following story, as if it were by Samuel's direction that Israel went out; had they consulted him, his counsel might have stood them in more stead than the presence of the ark did, but perhaps the princes of Israel despised his youth. What the clause means, on that reading, is that people from all parts who were piously disposed had recourse to him as a prophet; or else it refers to his prophecy against the house of Eli, which was generally known and talked of, so that the observing compared these events, when they came to pass, with the prophecy. Gill allows both senses and adds a third: the doctrine and exhortations of Samuel were conveyed throughout the land, and yet the people went into measures which proved fatal to them; or the word of Samuel, which was from the Lord, came to stir them up to go to war, whereby the punishment threatened to Eli's family began to have its accomplishment.

Ellicott takes the harder view, that the Hebrew revisers placed the notice as introducing the narrative of the battle, so that the war was begun at Samuel's word and the young prophet was mistaken in his first advice. He sets the error against the state of the nation. Anarchy and confusion had long prevailed throughout the tribes, and none of the Judges raised up so far had restored the stern theocracy that made the Israel of Moses and Joshua great; the high qualities which had raised Eli to the first place were in his old age almost totally obscured by a weak affection for his unworthy sons, and a terrible picture of the corruption of the priesthood belongs to the last period of his rule. In that moral degradation the Philistines, a warlike and enterprising race, made themselves supreme in many portions of the land. Samuel grew up in the midst of this, conscious that the invisible King had chosen him to restore the people, but he does not appear at first to have recognised how hopeless it was to attempt to free them from the Philistine yoke until something like a pure national religion was restored. Wesley reads the summons as a word of command, that all Israel should go forth to fight, that they might first be humbled and punished for their sins, and so prepared for deliverance.

Keil and Delitzsch state the whole issue of the campaign at the outset, and find its purpose in the humiliation it worked: the people were to learn that the Lord had departed from them, and Samuel also was to make the discovery that the deliverance of Israel from the oppression of its foes was impossible without its inward conversion. Henry judges the war itself an attempt to throw off the yoke of oppression which would have succeeded better if they had first repented and reformed, and so begun their work at the right end; he places it about the middle of the forty years of Philistine dominion and soon after the death of Samson, though he notes that Lightfoot reckons it forty years after. On the place-names both Clarke and Ellicott observe an anachronism. The name Eben-ezer, the stone of help, was not given until Samuel set up his monument after a signal victory some twenty years later; Clarke takes this for another proof that the book was compiled after the transactions it records, probably from memoranda made by a contemporary writer. Ellicott adds that the other name carries the article, the fortress, and may be the old Canaanite royal city of that name.
2:
Gill describes the challenge: the Philistines prepared for battle and put themselves in a posture for it, forming a line and so inviting Israel to fight. Keil and Delitzsch attend to one Hebrew phrase in the account of the loss — the four thousand were smitten in battle-array, that is, upon the field of battle and not in flight, and the field means the open ground where the battle was fought. Clarke draws two inferences from the number. There is no doubt that both the Philistines and the Israelites had what might be called the art of war, according to which they marshalled their troops, constructed their camps, and conducted their retreats and sieges, though we do not know the principles on which they acted; and this must have been a severe conflict, since four thousand were left dead on the field. It must also have lasted some considerable time, he adds, since these were all slain hand to hand, swords and spears being in all probability the only weapons then in use.

Keil and Delitzsch reconstruct the council that followed. On the return of the people to the camp the elders held a council of war as to the cause of the defeat, asking why Jehovah had smitten them; and since they had entered upon the war by the word and advice of Samuel, they were convinced that it was Jehovah who had smitten them. The question presupposes both that they felt strong enough to have entered the war and that the only possible reason for their defeat was that their covenant God had withdrawn his help — a correct conclusion, but the means they adopted to secure that help again were altogether wrong. Ellicott finds the same conclusion and the same failure: amazed at their defeat, they were puzzled to understand why God was evidently not in their midst, and showed by their next procedure how thoroughly they had gone astray from the old pure religion. Whether Samuel acquiesced in the fatal proposition we have no information; it evidently did not emanate from him, but, as we are expressly told, from the elders of the people. Wesley calls it strange blindness, that when there was so great a corruption in their worship and manners they could not see sufficient reason why God should suffer them to fall.

Clarke shows how the precedent was misread. They vainly supposed the ark could save them, when the God of it had departed from them because of their wickedness; they knew that their fathers had been beaten when they did not take the ark with them, as in the wars with the Canaanites, and had conquered when they did, as at the destruction of Jericho. From the latter case they took confidence, but the cause of their miscarriage in the former they laid not to heart. He notes too that it was customary with all the nations of the earth to take their gods and sacred ensigns with them to war, and that consecrated crosses and hallowed colours are the modern remains of those ancient superstitions. Ellicott calls it a curious delusion, this baseless hope that the unseen God was inseparably connected with a coffer of perishable wood and metal, and hears Jeremiah pressing the same lesson long afterwards upon a people slow to learn it: trust ye not in lying words, saying, the temple of the Lord. Wesley states the exchange they made: instead of humbling themselves for their sins and purging themselves from them, they take an easier and cheaper course and put their trust in ceremonial observances.
4:
Gill notes that the people liked the proposal of the elders and joined with them in a message to Eli the high priest at Shiloh. Ellicott sets against that errand what the errand assumed. There was, no doubt, in the minds of the elders the memory of many a glorious victory gained in the old heroic days of Moses and Joshua in the presence of the sacred Ark; but then God was with his people, and the Ark served as a reminder of his ever-presence, whereas now they had been disloyal to their unseen King, his very sanctuary had become infamous as a centre of vice, his ministers were chiefly known as prominent examples of covetousness and immorality, and the Ark had become only a symbol of the broken covenant. In vain was the grand battle hymn of Israel raised as in the old days when the Ark set forward, Rise up, Lord, and let thine enemies be scattered. The note that the two sons of Eli were there with it Ellicott finds sufficient by itself to account for the terrible discomfiture that followed: what a contrast the writer bitterly sets down, between the glorious but now deserted earthly throne of God and its guardians.

Clarke explains what the elders were counting on. Of what shape the cherubim were we do not know, but one of these figures was placed at each end of the ark, and between them, on the cover which was called the propitiatory or mercy-seat, the symbol of the divine presence was said to dwell; they thought therefore that if they had the ark, they must necessarily have the presence and influence of Jehovah. Keil and Delitzsch judge that this was probably the first time since the settlement in Canaan that the ark had been brought into the camp, so that the people anticipated from its presence a renewal of the marvellous victories gained under Moses and Joshua, and for that reason raised such a shout when it arrived that the earth rang again. Ellicott says the same and reads the shout as the confidence of the army that, now the Ark which had witnessed so many splendid victories was among them, discomfiture was out of the question. Clarke will not allow the shout even that much: had they humbled themselves and prayed devoutly and fervently for success, they would have been heard and saved, whereas their shouting proved both their vanity and their irreligion. Wesley draws the parallel — so formal Christians triumph in external privileges, as if the ark in the camp would bring them to heaven, though the world and the flesh reign in the heart.

The shout carried to the other camp, and Gill observes that it must have been loud indeed to make the earth ring and to be heard across the ground between, though how far Aphek stood from Eben-ezer is not certain. Keil and Delitzsch describe the alarm it caused. When the Philistines heard the noise, and learned on inquiry that the ark of Jehovah had come into the camp, they were thrown into consternation, saying that God was come into the camp, and crying woe to us, for such a thing has not happened yesterday nor the day before; who will deliver us from the hand of these mighty gods? They spoke of the God of Israel in the plural, as heathen who knew only of gods and not of one Almighty God; and just as all the heathen feared in some degree the might of the gods of other nations, so the Philistines were alarmed at the might of the God of the Israelites, and the more so because of the report that had reached them of what he had done in Egypt.
7:
Gill sets the scene: the spies returned and reported the reason of the shouting, and the Philistines were afraid. Clarke states the mistake shortly — they took for granted, as did the Israelites, that the presence of God was inseparable from his ark or shrine. Ellicott agrees that both peoples were equally superstitious in supposing that Deity was in some way connected with the lifeless gold and wood of the symbol; but he allows the Philistines some excuse for their fears, since tradition was no doubt current among the old inhabitants of Canaan how this sacred Ark had been carried before the conquering armies of Israel in many a battle and siege in those bygone days, when the strange shepherd hordes under Joshua first invaded and took possession of their beautiful land. Wesley narrows the words such a thing has not been heretofore to mean not in our times, since the earlier removals of the ark were before it came to rest at Shiloh. Ellicott locates the ground as well: the city near which the camp of Israel was pitched stood close to the western entrance of the Pass of Beth-horon, and the two defeats of Israel may be called the battles fought there.

The cry that follows is in the plural, and each commentator handles it differently. Gill thinks they may have spoken of the mighty gods in an ironical and sneering manner, or, if seriously and through fear, in their own heathenish language, as though the Israelites had many gods, as they themselves had, only mightier; he notes that the Syriac and Arabic read the singular, out of the hand of the most strong God, and the Targum, out of the hand of the Word of the Lord. Clarke would translate it in the singular too: who shall deliver us from the hand of this illustrious God? Ellicott keeps the plural and makes it evidence. He takes the words to be the very words of the Philistines, preserved in their national traditions, and the expression of idolaters who knew of gods and dreaded their malevolent influence but had no conception of the One Most High; the plural noun so often used in the sacred record for God is used here, but where the inspired compilers would have written the qualifying adjective in the singular, the Philistine idolaters write theirs in the plural. Wesley draws the moral of the cry: they secretly confess the Lord to be greater than their gods, and yet presume to oppose him.

On the plagues named, Ellicott observes that the Philistine exclamation is based outwardly upon the Egyptian traditions of the acts of the Lord, and that they studiedly ignore what everyone in that camp was painfully conscious of, his acts in their own land of Canaan. Some versions and commentators insert a word before the mention of the wilderness to bring the exclamation into harmony with history, since the plagues fell before Israel entered the wilderness; but Ellicott thinks the very vagueness of the cry speaks for its truth, since men in terror are little concerned with exact accuracy. Wesley solves the difficulty differently, taking the wilderness to be named not as the place of all the plagues but of the last and sorest of them, the destruction of Pharaoh and his host in the sea that has wilderness on both sides. Keil and Delitzsch describe what despair turned into: instead of giving way, they encouraged one another — show yourselves strong, and be men, that we may not be obliged to serve the Hebrews as they have served you. Clarke reports the threat implied, that if they did not acquit themselves like men the Hebrews would avenge upon them all the cruelty they had exercised; and Ellicott hears the ring of the same words afterwards in Paul's exhortation to the Corinthians, quit ye like men, be strong.
10:
Henry sets three contrasts in the rout. Israel was put to the worse though they had the better cause, being the people of God and standing up in defence of their just rights against invaders; yet they failed of success, for their rock had sold them: a good cause often suffers for the sake of the bad men that undertake it. They were put to the worse though they had the greater confidence and were the more courageous, since they shouted while the Philistines trembled, and yet the Philistines' terrors were turned into triumph and Israel's shouts into lamentation. And they were put to the worse though they had the ark of God with them, for external privileges will secure none that abuse them, and the ark in the camp will add nothing to its strength when there is an Achan in it. The dispersal was final: they did not retire into the camp, as after the first defeat, but returned to their tents, every man shifting for himself. Gill notes that the Philistines fought with great ardour and spirit, quitting themselves like men of valour, their case being as they imagined desperate, since God was in the camp of Israel.

Wesley marks the arithmetic of the two defeats: before, they lost four thousand; now, in the presence of the ark, thirty thousand — to teach them that the ark and the ordinances of God were never designed as a refuge for impenitent sinners, but only for the comfort of those who repent. Keil and Delitzsch take the loss of the ark and the death of Eli's sons together as a practical proof to the degenerate nation that Jehovah, who was enthroned above the cherubim, had departed from them and withdrawn his gracious presence. Ellicott traces the outcome to what he calls an immutable law in the connection of Israel with their God-Friend. So long as they clave to the invisible Preserver and served him with their whole heart, and kept themselves pure from the idol nations around them, so long was he in their midst and they were invincible; but when they chose to revel in the impure joys and shameless lives of the idolatrous world around them, and only carried the Ark upon their shoulders with no memory in their hearts of him whom the mercy-seat and the overshadowing cherubim symbolised, then, in the words of the hymn of Asaph, God was wroth and forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh, delivering his strength into captivity and his glory into the enemy's hand.

Ellicott notes that the bare fact of the capture is given without comment or note, though it was the greatest calamity that had yet happened to Israel; all the people would know by that terrible sign that their invisible King had withdrawn his countenance, while the loss of the Ark to the heathen taught another lesson besides, the eternal truth that the living God does not bind his presence to a dead thing. Yet, dead thing though it was, it was inexpressibly precious to the patriot: this was the ark which Moses had made at Sinai, which had accompanied Israel through the wilderness, before which Jordan had fled backward and the walls of Jericho had fallen. Gill gives two reasons for the permission: partly as punishment for fetching it from the tabernacle without the will of God and for their vain confidence in it, and partly that the Philistines might have experiment of his power by what they would suffer through having it among them. Of the priests Clarke says only that they probably attempted to defend the ark and lost their lives in the attempt, while Henry judges their slaughter, considering their character, no great loss to Israel, but a dreadful judgment upon the house of Eli, and the fulfilment of the word already spoken, that his two sons should die both in one day.
12:
Gill pictures the runner leaving the rank he stood in before the whole army was quite broken up, and takes him for a young man, as Josephus says, which is highly probable; the Jewish claim that this was Saul, later king of Israel, he thinks not at all to be depended on. Ellicott reports the same tradition, which adds that Saul snatched from Goliath the tables of the Law taken out of the Ark in order to save them, and then turns from the legend to the narrative itself: the whole account is so vivid, and so full of detail, that it must have come from some eye-witness, probably from Samuel. He observes that such swift runners are still employed to carry news in war time in the East, and gathers the parallels — Cushi and Ahimaaz bringing tidings from Joab to David, Asahel famous for his running, Elijah outrunning the chariot of Ahab between Carmel and Jezreel, and, outside Scripture, Phidippides reaching Sparta on the second day after leaving Athens. Clarke fixes the distance from the speed: the field of battle cannot have been at any great remove, since the young man reached Shiloh the same evening after the defeat.

Ellicott says only that the rent clothes and the earth upon the head were the usual indications that the news brought was of evil; Clarke makes them a study. These were signs of sorrow and distress among all nations: the rent clothes signified the rending and dividing and scattering of the people, the earth or ashes on the head their humiliation — we are brought down to the dust of the earth, we are near to our graves. He then ranges through the poets for the same gestures. In Virgil, Aeneas tears the robe from his shoulders and calls the gods to help when the Trojan fleet is burnt; the queen of Latinus, resolving on her own death, rends her purple vest; and Latinus himself, hearing of her death and seeing his city in flames, tears his garments and defiles his silver hairs with dust. Catullus has the same in a single line. In Homer the Greeks shear the curling honours of their heads over the dead, and Achilles, hearing of the death of Patroclus, casts the scorching ashes over his own. Clarke ends nearer home: even in the most civilised parts of Europe it is not unusual to see grief expressed by tearing the hair, beating the breasts and rending the garments, these being natural signs common to all the nations of the world.

Henry follows the news to the one place that had most to lose. Bad news flies fast, and this soon spread through all Israel, every man that fled to his tent bringing it with too plain a proof to his neighbours; but no place was so nearly concerned as Shiloh, and thither an express posted away immediately. The messenger was loath to tell Eli first, and therefore passed him by and told it in the city with all its aggravating circumstances; and now both the ears of every one that heard it tingled, as had been foretold, their hearts trembled, and every face gathered blackness. All the city cried out, and well they might, for besides the calamity to all Israel this was the ruin of that place. Though the ark was soon rescued out of the hands of the Philistines, it never returned to Shiloh again; their candlestick was removed out of its place because they had left their first love, and their city dwindled and sank and came to nothing. The tribe of Ephraim, which had for centuries been blessed with the presence of the ark, lost the honour, and it was in time transferred to Judah; and long afterwards Jerusalem is bidden to take warning by it — go see what I did to Shiloh.
13:
Gill supposes the runner either passed by Eli, who being blind could not see him, or came in at another gate on the other side of the city; the first seems the likelier, since he did not choose to deliver such news to Eli first and slipped by into the city. Ellicott would render the description of Eli's post more exactly: he sat by the side of the way of the watchers, that is, the street in Shiloh so named probably from the watch-tower situated in it; the Septuagint has it, by the side of the gate watching the way. The old judge was naturally anxious for news from the army, since the people had already suffered a great reverse in the first battle; but his chief anxiety was for the sacred Ark which he had allowed, no doubt against his better judgment, to leave the sanctuary. Ellicott credits him with more insight than the elders had: Eli knew too much of the Eternal Guardian of Israel to put any real trust in the power of a lifeless Ark, and knew well how long it was since the glory had rested on its golden mercy-seat between the silent cherubim, so that he waited with sorrowful forebodings, asking himself whether the Ark would ever return to Shiloh.

Clarke states the paradox in the old man's fear: he was a most mild and affectionate father, and yet the safety of the ark lay nearer to his heart than the safety of his two sons — who can help feeling for this aged, venerable man? Wesley reads the same trembling as the mark of a public and generous spirit and a fervent zeal for God's honour, which Eli preferred before all his natural affections, not regarding his own children in comparison of the ark, though otherwise he was a most indulgent father. Gill notes that Eli had his hearing though not his sight: he could not see the distress in their countenances, but he heard the shrieks of the men and women, which were very clamorous and terrible. Ellicott fills in the scene around him — the blind old man seated on his chair of state, surrounded by the priests and Levites in attendance on him as high priest and judge; as the runner drew near and the torn dress and the sprinkled dust became visible, the wail of woe would run through the place, and the cry of sorrow was the first intimation to Eli, whose question was probably addressed in the first place to the little court standing by his throne.

The note of Eli's age is given a medical and a textual gloss. Keil and Delitzsch read the Hebrew as saying that his eyes stood, that is, were stiff, so that he could no longer see, and identify the condition as the so-called black cataract, which generally occurs at a very great age from paralysis of the optic nerves. Ellicott adopts the same rendering and the same diagnosis, and adds a caution about the figure itself: the Septuagint reads ninety here and the Syriac seventy-eight, and where numbers are concerned we usually find such varieties, since the Hebrews used the letters of the alphabet to express them, a system naturally fruitful in errors of transcription, so that numbers and dates in the earlier books are frequently confused. Many of the difficulties which have given commentators so much trouble have arisen from copyists substituting one letter for another through inadvertence. Gill observes that the age is very properly noted at this point, Eli being now come to the end of his days, and that it also accounts for the blindness afterwards mentioned. Ellicott adds that the fatal battle had taken place very early that same morning, and that the very words of the runner were remembered, the scene having evidently been related by a bystander.
17:
Gill commends the messenger's method: he delivered his account gradually, beginning with generals and then proceeding to particulars, and with what he thought Eli could better bear, so preparing him for the worst — in which he acted a wise part. Clarke says never was a more afflictive message, containing such a variety of woes, each rising above the preceding, delivered in so few words, and numbers them. Israel is fled before the Philistines: that Israel should turn their backs on their enemies was bad, and that they should turn them on such enemies as these was worse, for now they might expect the chains of their slavery to be riveted more closely. There has been a great slaughter: a rout might have happened without one, but here the field was warmly contested, and the flower of their armies was destroyed. Thy two sons are dead: more afflictive still to a father who lost both the hope of his house, and by a violent death when there was so little prospect of their having died in the peace of God. And the ark of God is taken: the most dreadful of the whole, since Israel is now dishonoured in the sight of the heathen.

The brevity of the message strikes Clarke as art, and then as something better than art. How high does each woe rise on the back of the preceding, and with what apparent skill is this laconic report constructed — and yet probably no skill at all was used, the messenger delivering the tidings just as the facts rose up in his own mind. He sets it beside the speech in which Aeschylus makes a runner bring the queen of Persia news of the ruin of her navy, and finds that diffuse by comparison; then beside three famous brevities of commanders: the three words in which Caesar reported the defeat of Pharnaces, the sentence in which Admiral Hawke told his king he had taken, burnt and destroyed the French fleet as per margin, and the note Bonaparte sent his wife before attacking Alvinzi. Excellent as these are, Clarke says, each contains little more than one idea, whereas the Benjamite's report includes several — the general and the particular disasters of the day, the rout, the great slaughter, the death of the priests who were in effect the whole generals of the army, and the capture of the ark — and does it in four simple assertions.

Only the last word killed him. Gill says the rest he bore tolerably well — the flight of Israel, the great slaughter, the death of his two sons — but the taking of the ark was so dreadful to him that he could not support under it. Keil and Delitzsch say the same: at that news he fell back from his seat by the side of the gate and broke his neck and died, the loss of the ark being to him more dreadful than the death of his sons. Of the length of his rule they will not entertain the shorter reading of the Septuagint, since it is incredible that Eli was made judge in his seventy-eighth year; Clarke notes that all the other versions, and the Hebrew, have the longer term. Ellicott finds the scene the more convincing because the compiler nowhere spares Eli, never veiling his weakness or his blind nepotism. He could bear the announcement of the ruin of his proud house, could see the boy Samuel preferred before him, could hear of the defeat of the country he had ruled so long, could listen with sad resignation even to the death of his sons; but when his ears caught the words that the ark was taken, the old man's heart broke. Wesley makes the exclamation for him: let me fall with the ark, for who can live when the ordinances of God are removed?
19:
Henry finds two things in the woman: a very tender spirit and a very gracious one. Providence ordered it that just at this juncture she was near her time, and the amazing news put her into labour, as great frights or other strong passions sometimes do; hearing of the death of the father-in-law she reverenced and the husband whom, bad as he was, she loved, but chiefly of the capture, her pains came thickly upon her; and though she had strength to bear the child she fainted and died soon after, willing to let life go when its greatest comforts were gone. Her concern for the death of husband and father-in-law was evidence of natural affection, but her much greater concern for the ark was evidence of a devout affection to God and to sacred things; and it appears by her dying words that the latter lay nearer her heart, since she laments not so much the sinking of the family she was related to as the general calamity of Israel. Gill lingers on the Hebrew for her nearness to delivery — some derive it from a root meaning to complete, so that her time was filled up, while Moses Kimchi derives it from a root meaning to howl, and so of a woman crying out when her pains come.

The comfort offered her fell flat. Wesley grants that the sorrows of her travail would ordinarily have been forgotten for joy that a child was born into the world, and then asks what that joy is to one who feels herself dying: none but spiritual joy will stand us in stead then, for death admits not the relish of any earthly joy, which is then all flat and tasteless. And what is it to one bereaved of the ark? What can please us if we want God's word and ordinances, and the light of his countenance? Henry adds that the women attending her, likely of the first rank in the city, supposed her concern was only for the issue of her pains, and so bade her fear not, since she had borne a son; but she answered not, neither did she regard it. Small comfort could she take in a child born in Israel, in Shiloh, when the ark was a prisoner in the land of the Philistines. Clarke says it shortly: that information she regarded not.

The name she gave is read three ways. Gill reports that some render it, where is the glory, as the margin of our Bibles has it, but that Jarchi and Kimchi interpret it as no glory; her husband being dead, it fell to her to name the child. Clarke surveys the ancient versions and finds them various and unhelpful, so that we are left to collect the meaning from what she says afterwards; the words literally mean, where is the glory — and indeed where was it, he asks, when the armies of Israel were defeated, the priests slain, the supreme magistrate dead, and the ark of the Lord taken? Henry hears in the name a memorial meant to outlast her: call the child inglorious, for so he is, the beauty of Israel being lost with no hope of retrieving it. The purity and plenty of God's ordinances, and the tokens of his presence in them, are the glory of any people, much more than their wealth or trade or standing among the nations; and nothing is more cutting to a faithful Israelite than to want them, for if God go, the glory goes, and all good goes. Wesley notes that the reason is repeated at the last to show her piety, and that the public loss lay heavier on her spirit than her own domestic calamity.
